meta.title: Who really said "Maybe you'll fail most of the time, but until you've dared to try and have brought off an impossible shot from the rough or from the water, you haven't really tasted the game"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Arnold Palmer wrote it — but the documented sentence in My Game and Yours (1965) ends differently. The circulating tail has no source we could find.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Maybe you'll fail most of the time, but until you've dared to try and have brought off an impossible shot from the rough or from the water, you haven't really tasted the game'?
meta.ogDescription: Palmer’s line is cited to My Game and Yours (1965), p. 83 — where it ends on a 2-iron, not on “tasted the game”.

answer.label: Palmer’s line — but not in these words
answer.sourceLine: Arnold Palmer did write this — but not with this ending. Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ places the sentence in My Game and Yours (1965) at page 83, and the sentence it documents runs on past “from the water”: “… or have salvaged a hole by laying a monster of a 2-iron shot stiff against the pin, you will have missed golf’s greatest playing thrill.” The closing clause in circulation — “you haven’t really tasted the game” — turns up in no source we could reach, including the page that carries the citation.

source.heading: The source, and where the wording parts company

docMeta.dd: 83 — per Wikiquote’s citation; the book is in copyright and we did not read the page ourselves

source.excerpt: Maybe you’ll fail most of the time, but until you’ve dared to try and have brought off an impossible shot from the rough or from the water, or have salvaged a hole by laying a monster of a 2-iron shot stiff against the pin, you will have missed golf’s greatest playing thrill.
trail: The wording comes from Wikiquote’s Arnold Palmer page ↗, where the sentence sits in the sourced section with a book citation attached: My Game and Yours, 1965, page 83.
The book exists as cited. The Internet Archive’s catalogue record for My game and yours ↗ gives Palmer, Arnold, 1929–; New York, Simon and Schuster; 1965; 158 p.

We searched for the circulating ending — “you haven’t really tasted the game” — and found nothing carrying it: not the Wikiquote entry that supplies the citation, and not any collection we could reach. On that evidence it is a later paraphrase, and we say so rather than printing it as Palmer’s sentence.

What we could not do, stated plainly: the 1965 text is in copyright and the Archive’s scan is lending-restricted, so page 83 was not read here. The documented wording rests on Wikiquote’s sourced citation alone.

author.name: Arnold Palmer
author.heading: About Arnold Palmer
author.bio: Arnold Daniel Palmer (1929–2016) was an American professional golfer, widely regarded as one of the greatest and most charismatic players in the sport’s history. He turned professional in 1955 and won repeatedly on the PGA Tour and on the circuit now known as PGA Tour Champions. Nicknamed “the King”, he was golf’s first superstar of the television age, and the attacking, go-for-it style that made him famous is exactly what this sentence is defending.

misattribution.heading: Often mis-worded
misattribution.intro: Nobody else is claiming this line. What happened to it is simpler: the ending fell off and a smoother one grew back.

items.why: The documented sentence does not stop at the water hazard. It adds a third clause — the 2-iron laid stiff against the pin — and closes “you will have missed golf’s greatest playing thrill.” See Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗, which carries the book and page. The tidier ending in circulation is not in it.

The sentiment and the sentence are his. Wikiquote ↗ files the line under a real book with a page number, and the Internet Archive’s catalogue record for that book ↗ matches the citation. This page corrects a wording, not an attribution.

misattribution.truthLine: Best evidence: Arnold Palmer, My Game and Yours (New York: Simon and Schuster, 1965), page 83, as cited by Wikiquote ↗ — ending on the 2-iron, not on “tasted the game”.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Palmer turned professional in 1955 and became, as Wikipedia ↗ puts it, the first superstar of golf’s television age — nicknamed “the King” and widely regarded as one of the most charismatic players the sport has had.

That is the context the sentence belongs to. It is not a motivational slogan about trying hard; it is a working player’s defence of the reckless recovery shot, the one that fails most of the time, written by the man whose attacking style was the reason crowds followed him.
detailsBody: My Game and Yours was published by Simon and Schuster in 1965, a 158-page instruction book, a decade into Palmer’s professional career. The Internet Archive holds a lending scan ↗; Wikiquote’s citation points into a Google Books copy ↗ of the same volume.

Why we did not simply call this “verified”: the page’s whole job is the exact wording, and the exact wording asked about is not the documented one. Calling it verified would endorse an ending no source carries.
context.pull: Maybe you’ll fail most of the time — and that is the argument, not the caveat.
